lead: A cell turns a chemical redox reaction into electrical work by splitting it into two half-reactions held apart. Each half-reaction sits on its own metal electrode dipped in its own ion solution, and each has a single electrode potential. Join the electrodes with a wire and the solutions with a salt bridge, and electrons flow. The cell EMF is the difference between the two electrode potentials. Phone batteries, the corrosion cell on a wet gate and every pH meter reading rest on this one idea, so the sign conventions must be handled carefully.
prereq: You need: school-level redox and oxidation numbers (see Unit 1, Chemical Bonding and Coordination Compounds, for oxidation states in complexes).

blocks.text: A galvanic cell (some syllabi say voltaic cell) converts the energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electricity. Drop zinc into copper sulphate solution and zinc dissolves while copper plates out, but the energy leaves as heat and no current flows. Keep the two half-reactions in separate compartments and the same electron transfer must push through an outside wire. That separation is the whole trick.

In the Daniell cell, a zinc rod stands in 1 M ZnSO₄ and a copper rod stands in 1 M CuSO₄. Zinc oxidises: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻. This electrode is the anode, where oxidation happens. Copper ions reduce: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu. This electrode is the cathode, where reduction happens. Electrons leave zinc, travel through the wire and reach copper; conventional current flows the opposite way.

A salt bridge is a tube of KCl set in agar gel that joins the two solutions. Positive ions move towards the cathode compartment and negative ions towards the anode compartment. It closes the circuit and keeps both solutions electrically neutral without letting them mix. Without it, charge builds up at the electrodes within microseconds and the cell stops.

items: Write the anode half-cell on the left and the cathode half-cell on the right.
Use a single vertical bar | for a phase boundary, such as metal | solution.
Use a double bar || for the salt bridge.
Write the concentration after each species: Zn | Zn²⁺ (1 M) || Cu²⁺ (1 M) | Cu.

sections.h3: Single electrode potential and the hydrogen zero

blocks.text: A metal dipped in a solution of its own ions develops a potential difference across the metal–solution interface. Two opposing tendencies act: metal atoms dissolve as ions and leave electrons on the metal, and ions from the solution deposit back on the metal. When the two rates become equal, a steady charge separation sits at the surface. That potential difference is the single electrode potential of the couple.

A single electrode potential cannot be measured alone, because a voltmeter needs a second terminal. Every electrode potential is therefore measured against a chosen reference, the standard hydrogen electrode (SHE). The SHE is a platinum foil coated with platinum black, dipped in 1 M H⁺ solution, with H₂ gas bubbled at 1 bar, at 298 K. Its half-reaction is 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ ⇌ H₂. By convention its potential is fixed at exactly 0.00 V.

blocks.where: E° is the standard electrode potential in volts; the H⁺ activity is 1 and the H₂ pressure is 1 bar at 298 K.

blocks.text: Standard conditions are 298 K, 1 bar for gases, 1 M for dissolved species (strictly, unit activity) and a pure electrode. Under these conditions the measured value is a standard electrode potential, written E°. The sign tells you the direction: E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V, so zinc is less noble than hydrogen and its half-cell tends to oxidise, giving electrons away. E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, so copper tends to reduce and take electrons.

sections.h3: The electrochemical series and cell EMF

blocks.text: Arrange couples by E° and you get the electrochemical series. The more negative the value, the more active the metal and the stronger its tendency to oxidise. A metal high in the series displaces a metal below it from its salt solution: zinc displaces copper, copper does not displace zinc. When two metals touch in a conducting liquid, the more negative one becomes the anode and corrodes (see Unit 4, corrosion).

blocks.where: E°cell is the standard cell EMF in volts, E°cathode is the standard potential of the couple that reduces, and E°anode is the standard potential of the couple that oxidises, each taken with its own sign.

blocks.text: When you combine two couples, the one with the more positive E° becomes the cathode if the cell runs spontaneously. A positive E°cell means the reaction as written is spontaneous and the cell delivers that voltage on open circuit. These values hold only at standard conditions; change a concentration and the potential shifts, which is the Nernst equation in 4.2.

figure.caption: Zinc oxidises and releases Zn²⁺ while electrons leave through the wire; the KCl salt bridge carries ion current, and Cu²⁺ gains electrons at the copper strip. Notice that both solutions are 1 M, which is what makes these standard potentials.

spec.title: Daniell cell
spec.aria: A zinc electrode in 1 M zinc ion solution connects through a KCl salt bridge to 1 M copper ion solution and a copper electrode.

examples.question: For the Daniell cell Zn | Zn²⁺ (1 M) || Cu²⁺ (1 M) | Cu at 298 K, the standard electrode potentials are E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V and E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V. (a) Write the anode and cathode half-reactions. (b) Calculate the standard cell EMF.
steps: Identify the couple that oxidises. Zinc has the more negative potential, so zinc is the anode: Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻.
The copper couple reduces at the cathode: Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu.
Write the formula: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode.
Substitute with signs: E°cell = (+0.34 V) − (−0.76 V).
Check the sign: E°cell is positive, so the cell reaction is spontaneous as written.
examples.answer: The cell EMF is E°cell = 1.10 V, with zinc as anode and copper as cathode.
examples.check:
zn = -0.76
cu = 0.34
e_cell = cu - zn
print(round(e_cell, 2))

traps: Do not add the two electrode potentials with their signs and then forget the anode sign. Use E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode; the zinc electrode enters as −0.76 V, not +0.76 V.
The anode is the negative terminal in a galvanic cell but the positive terminal in an electrolytic cell. In both, oxidation still happens at the anode.
Reversing a half-reaction flips the sign of E°, but doubling the half-reaction does not double E°. Potential is intensive; only ΔG and n scale.
The salt bridge is not a wire. Electrons travel through the metal wire; the bridge carries ions and only completes the circuit.
E° = 0.00 V belongs to the SHE only: 1 M H⁺, 1 bar H₂, 298 K, platinum black. A bare platinum wire in dilute acid is not a hydrogen electrode.

quiz.q: Define anode and cathode for a galvanic cell.
quiz.a: The anode is the electrode where oxidation occurs and electrons are released; the cathode is the electrode where reduction occurs and electrons are consumed.

quiz.q: State the four conditions that define the standard hydrogen electrode.
quiz.a: Platinum foil coated with platinum black, H⁺ at 1 M activity, H₂ gas at 1 bar, temperature 298 K; E° is fixed at 0.00 V by convention.

quiz.q: Why is a salt bridge needed in the Daniell cell?
quiz.a: It carries ions between the two compartments, keeps each solution electrically neutral, completes the circuit and prevents the two solutions from mixing directly.

quiz.q: Why can the absolute single electrode potential of a zinc electrode not be measured?
quiz.a: A potential difference needs two terminals. Any voltmeter or cell used to measure it adds a second electrode, so only the difference between two electrode potentials is measured. Hence all values are referred to the SHE, taken as zero.

quiz.q: E°(Ag⁺/Ag) = +0.80 V and E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V. Calculate E°cell for Zn | Zn²⁺ (1 M) || Ag⁺ (1 M) | Ag.
quiz.a: Zinc is the anode and silver the cathode. E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.80 − (−0.76) = 1.56 V. Positive, so the reaction is spontaneous.

quiz.q: Two couples are Sn²⁺/Sn with E° = −0.14 V and Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ with E° = +0.77 V. Which acts as cathode when they form a cell?
quiz.a: The more positive couple becomes the cathode, so Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ is the cathode and Sn²⁺/Sn the anode. E°cell = 0.77 − (−0.14) = 0.91 V.

quiz.q: A student computes the Daniell cell EMF as (−0.76) + (+0.34) = −0.42 V and concludes the cell is not spontaneous. Identify the error and give the correct value.
quiz.a: Adding both potentials ignores that one couple oxidises. The formula is E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V. The negative result came from subtracting in the wrong order, and the true E°cell is positive, so the cell is spontaneous.

quiz.q: Using the electrochemical series, predict whether a zinc strip placed in 1 M CuSO₄ will dissolve, and explain with potentials.
quiz.a: Yes. E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) = −0.76 V is more negative than E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V, so zinc oxidises to Zn²⁺ and Cu²⁺ reduces to copper. E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.76) = 1.10 V, positive, so the displacement is spontaneous and the zinc strip loses mass.

beyond: Not for the exam. The SHE is awkward to build and keep pure, so laboratories work with secondary references such as Ag/AgCl or calomel, whose potentials are themselves fixed against the SHE. Computational electrochemistry now estimates standard potentials from density functional theory with solvent models and checks them against measured series. Ion-selective electrodes for fluoride or nitrate, and the reference inside every pH meter, calibrate against the same zero. Battery and corrosion engineers screen new metal couples by looking up standard potentials first. Useful searches: standard electrode potential tables, Ag/AgCl reference electrode, computational standard potentials.
